title: Self Assessment for Sole Traders: What You Need for Your 2025/26 Tax Return
excerpt: What self-employed sole traders should gather for the 2025 to 2026 Self Assessment return — sales, expenses, other income, filing steps and deadlines.
metaTitle: Sole Trader Tax Return 2025/26: Records to Prepare | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Prepare your 2025/26 sole-trader tax return with sales, platform reports, expenses, equipment details and other income organised for your accountant.
featuredImageAlt: A sole trader closes a yearly accounts folder with receipts, equipment evidence and an orderly ledger.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Deadlines
GOV.UK — Check how to register for Self Assessment
GOV.UK — Understand your Self Assessment tax bill: Payments on account

content:
If you traded as a sole trader in 2025 to 2026, your Self Assessment return needs a clear picture of sales, allowable expenses and anything else taxable that year. This page is Self Assessment preparation, not the Making Tax Digital sole-trader checklist (that is MTD for sole traders 2026/27), and not a generic document dump (see the documents checklist for the wide list).

Income and sales evidence

  • Invoices or sales reports for the tax year (6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026)
  • Bank statements for the business account (or highlighted personal-account business lines)
  • Platform payouts (marketplaces, card readers) reconciled to invoices
  • CIS statements if you are a subcontractor
  • Any tips, grants or other trading receipts

Business expenses worth sorting early

Group costs the way your accountant will ask for them: stock or materials, subcontractors, premises, vehicle/travel, office costs, professional fees, insurance, phone/internet used for the trade, and capital purchases that may need capital allowances. Private spending mixed into the same account needs a clear split. “I’ll remember in January” is how allowable claims get lost.

A concrete prep example

Maya is a freelance photographer. For 2025 to 2026 she has invoices totalling £42,600, equipment hire and props of £3,150, software subscriptions of £480, train travel to shoots of £920, and a new camera body costing £1,800 that may need capital-allowance treatment rather than a simple expense. She exports bank CSV files and keeps PDF invoices in one folder labelled by month. That pack is enough for an accountant to draft the trade pages without reconstructing the year from memory.

Other income and the rest of the return

Sole-trader profit is rarely the whole story. Note employment income, taxable benefits, dividends, savings interest, rental income, pension contributions, and student loan indicators. Payments on account from the previous year also affect what you pay by 31 January. See payments on account explained.

Accountant workflow, approval and deadlines

Online return and balancing payment for 2025 to 2026: 31 January 2027. Paper deadline: 31 October 2026. If you still need to register or reactivate Self Assessment for this year, check the 5 October 2026 notification date.

TaxSimba’s Self Assessment service is accountant-led: you supply the records, an accountant prepares the return, you approve, then it is filed. We do not sell DIY filing software or promise a fixed tax saving.

Put it into practice

Reconcile platform sales with payouts

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

Ellis records £12,000 of customer sales through a card platform, £300 of platform fees and £11,700 paid to his bank. Treating the payout alone as sales would conceal the fee and weaken the trail. He supplies the sales report, fee breakdown and bank entries, then identifies cash sales separately. He also lists a new laptop with its purchase date and business-use split, so the accountant can check the treatment under his accounting basis rather than automatically applying capital allowances.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Do recorded sales include cash and platform fees?Reconcile gross customer receipts to net payouts without counting transfers twice.
Which accounting basis applies?Confirm cash basis or traditional accounting before allocating dates and equipment costs.
Is the personal return complete?Include employment, savings, property and relevant relief information as well as the trade.

Two more questions you may have

Is the business bank statement enough?

It is useful evidence, but it may omit cash, hide platform deductions or include private transfers. Supply the sales and expense records behind it.

Does every equipment purchase need capital allowances?

No. Treatment depends on the asset and accounting basis. Keep the invoice and business-use details so the appropriate rules can be applied.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Confirm the tax year and accounting basis.
  • Reconcile bank, cash and platform sales.
  • Group expenses and mark private-use shares.
  • List equipment purchases and disposals.
  • Gather other income, reliefs and prior payments.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: Do I Need to Register for Self Assessment by 5 October 2026?
excerpt: 5 October 2026 is the date to tell HMRC you need a Self Assessment tax return for 2025 to 2026 if you are new to filing or need to reactivate — not the same as the 31 January filing deadline.
metaTitle: Missed 5 October 2026? Self Assessment Registration | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check who had to notify HMRC by 5 October 2026, what to do if you missed it and why a revised filing deadline does not move the tax payment date.
featuredImageAlt: A new freelancer checks a registration acknowledgement and official letter while an adviser checks two separate deadline notes.

before.title: Do I Need to Register for Self Assessment by 5 October 2026?
before.metaDescription: Check who must notify HMRC by 5 October 2026 about a 2025/26 Self Assessment return, and keep registration, filing and payment deadlines separate.

after.title: Missed the 5 October Self Assessment Registration Date? Here’s What to Do
after.metaTitle: Missed 5 October 2026? Self Assessment Registration | TaxSimba
after.metaDescription: Check who had to notify HMRC by 5 October 2026, what to do if you missed it and why a revised filing deadline does not move the tax payment date.
after.excerpt: Check who had to notify HMRC by 5 October 2026, what to do if you missed it and why a revised filing deadline does not move the tax payment date.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Check how to register for Self Assessment
GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Deadlines
GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Registering for Self Assessment

content:
Not everyone must “register by 5 October.” GOV.UK’s rule is narrower: you must tell HMRC by 5 October 2026 if you need to complete a tax return for the previous tax year (2025 to 2026: 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026) and you have either:

  • not sent a tax return before, or
  • registered before but did not need to send a tax return for 2024 to 2025

You tell HMRC by registering for Self Assessment (or by following the reactivation path inside that service if you already had an account). Check whether you need a return before you register.

The 5 October 2026 notification date has passed. GOV.UK required people to tell HMRC by that date if they needed a tax return for 2025 to 2026 and had either never sent a return, or had registered before but did not need a return for 2024 to 2025. If that described you and you have not told HMRC yet, register or reactivate now. Waiting does not remove the need to file or pay.

What 5 October is, and is not

5 October is a tell HMRC / registration (or reactivation) date for people in those two situations. It is not the deadline for submitting the tax return or paying the bill.

  • Online return and payment: 11:59pm on 31 January 2027
  • Paper return: 11:59pm on 31 October 2026

People who already file Self Assessment every year are not suddenly given a new universal “re-register by 5 October” duty. Use GOV.UK’s “check how to register” flow if you are unsure which path applies, including reactivation if you skipped 2024 to 2025.

If you miss 5 October 2026

GOV.UK warns you could get a penalty if you tell HMRC after 5 October 2026. If you register after that date, HMRC will send a letter or email with a different deadline to send your tax return (three months from the date on that letter or email). You must still pay any tax owed by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027 or you can get a payment penalty. More on late filing generally: late Self Assessment penalties.

If you are registering after 5 October 2026

GOV.UK says you could get a penalty for telling HMRC late. After a late registration, HMRC will send a letter or email with a revised deadline to send your tax return (three months from the date on that letter or email). You must still pay any tax owed by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027 or you can get a payment penalty. Practical catch-up reading: late Self Assessment penalties.

Practical next steps

  1. Confirm you actually need a 2025 to 2026 return (GOV.UK’s “check if you need to send a tax return” tool).
  2. Use Check how to register for Self Assessment on GOV.UK, including reactivation where relevant.
  3. Gather records early so the January filing date is not a scramble (documents checklist).
  4. Diary 31 January 2027 for online filing and payment.

If you want an accountant to prepare the return once you are registered, TaxSimba’s Self Assessment service is accountant-led from your documents. We cannot register you with HMRC in place of the GOV.UK process, and we do not guarantee penalty cancellation. Re-check GOV.UK for the wording that applies to you.

Put it into practice

Registration and payment need separate dates

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

Clara realises in October 2026 that her 2025/26 trading income requires a return and she has never filed before. She registers promptly, gathers the records and retains HMRC's acknowledgement. If HMRC gives her a revised filing deadline after late registration, she records that exact date. She also keeps 31 January 2027 on the payment plan: a later return deadline does not automatically defer tax. An adviser checks any failure-to-notify exposure from the full facts.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Do you actually need a 2025/26 return?Use the official checker and identify the income or other reason before choosing a registration route.
New registration or reactivation?Follow HMRC's route for your existing record rather than creating duplicate registrations.
What does HMRC's notice say?Record the specific filing deadline and keep the payment deadline separately.

Two more questions you may have

Does everyone re-register every October?

No. The notification rule targets people who need a return and have not filed before, or need to reactivate after a year without a required return.

Should I wait until January if I missed October?

No. Tell HMRC promptly and prepare records now. Check any revised filing deadline and the tax payment date rather than assuming more time for both.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Record why a return is required.
  • Check prior Self Assessment registration and filing history.
  • Submit the correct registration or reactivation request.
  • Retain HMRC's acknowledgement and filing date.
  • Plan tax payment independently from filing.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: I Cannot Pay My Self Assessment Tax Bill — What Should I Do?
excerpt: If you cannot pay your Self Assessment bill in full, GOV.UK sets out payment plans for overdue tax and Budget Payment Plans for upcoming bills. Here is how to tell which path fits and what to do next.
metaTitle: Cannot Pay Your Self Assessment Bill? Next Steps | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check your Self Assessment balance, distinguish a payment plan from advance budgeting and prepare affordability information before contacting HMRC.
featuredImageAlt: A taxpayer discusses a realistic household budget and tax bill with a supportive adviser; no money exchange or despair.

sources.label: GOV.UK — If you cannot pay your tax bill on time: Overview
GOV.UK — If you cannot pay your tax bill on time: Setting up a payment plan
GOV.UK — Pay your Self Assessment tax bill: Pay weekly or monthly
GOV.UK — Pay your Self Assessment tax bill: Overview

content:
Self Assessment payment dates do not move just because cash is tight. Balancing payments and the first payment on account are usually due by midnight on 31 January, with the second payment on account due by midnight on 31 July. If you cannot clear the balance in one go, GOV.UK still expects you to act early rather than hope the bill disappears.

First, work out which problem you have

There are two common situations, and they are not the same tool on GOV.UK:

  • The bill is overdue, or you cannot pay what you already owe. You may be able to set up a payment plan (often called a Time to Pay arrangement) to pay an overdue Self Assessment debt in monthly instalments, if HMRC agrees it is affordable.
  • You are not overdue yet, but January or July will be hard. If you are up to date with your last Self Assessment bill, you may be able to set up a Budget Payment Plan: weekly or monthly Direct Debit payments towards your next bill so less is left at the deadline.

GOV.UK also has a checker for which regular-payment option may be available. Use that before you guess.

If you cannot pay an overdue Self Assessment bill

HMRC’s “cannot pay on time” guidance says you may be able to pay in instalments. HMRC will check whether a plan is affordable. If you cannot agree a plan, they can still ask you to pay the full amount.

To set up a plan online you will usually need:

  • your Self Assessment payment reference (your 10-digit UTR followed by the letter K)
  • UK bank details you are authorised to use for Direct Debit
  • a clear picture of income and spending

If you cannot set a plan up online, contact HMRC and be ready to say whether you can pay in full, how much you can repay each month, what other tax you owe, what you earn and spend, and what savings or investments you hold. GOV.UK is clear that HMRC will expect you to use savings or assets to reduce the debt where you can. Independent debt advice documents such as a Standard Financial Statement can help evidence affordability.

If the bill is still ahead of you

A Budget Payment Plan is for people who are up to date on the last Self Assessment bill and want to drip-feed money towards the next one. You choose weekly or monthly amounts in your HMRC account under Direct Debit. You can pause payments for up to six months if you need to. If the plan does not cover the whole bill, you still pay the difference by the usual deadline. If you overpay, you can ask for a refund.

What not to do

Do not ignore letters or your online balance. Late payment can attract interest, and unpaid tax can attract late payment penalties on top. Filing on time still matters even while you arrange payment. Late filing penalties are a separate problem covered in late Self Assessment penalties.

Also check whether part of what looks “unpayable” is actually a payment on account that should be reduced because this year’s income is lower. That is a different process: how to reduce payments on account.

Practical sequence that usually helps

  1. Sign in and read the current balance and due dates, not just the paper letter.
  2. Separate balancing payment, payments on account, interest and penalties in your head (or on paper).
  3. Use GOV.UK’s payment-plan tools for overdue tax, or a Budget Payment Plan if you are still ahead of the deadline and up to date.
  4. Pay something you can afford through an official channel if a full plan is not ready yet, using the correct payment reference.
  5. Keep filing and record-keeping moving so the next bill is based on accurate figures.

If the underlying return still needs preparing, TaxSimba’s Self Assessment service is accountant-led from the records you supply. We cannot promise that HMRC will accept a particular payment plan, waive interest, or cancel penalties. Payment arrangements are between you and HMRC on GOV.UK’s terms.

Put it into practice

A realistic plan starts with the actual balance

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

Imran expects a £3,600 amount to remain unpaid after the deadline. Before asking HMRC for instalments, he checks whether it includes balancing tax, advance payments, interest or penalties. He prepares a monthly income-and-spending summary and lists other debts and available savings. He continues the return work while discussing payment. An affordable proposal supports the conversation, but it is not an agreed Time to Pay arrangement until HMRC confirms the terms.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Is the tax overdue or still ahead?Use the appropriate official payment-plan or advance-budgeting route for your position.
Can you evidence an affordable amount?Prepare income, essential spending, assets and other tax debts before contacting HMRC.
Is the return still outstanding?Progress filing separately so payment difficulties do not create an avoidable filing problem.

Two more questions you may have

Does paying something mean HMRC accepted a plan?

No. A payment reduces the balance but does not itself establish an instalment arrangement. Retain the confirmation and terms of any agreed plan.

Can reducing payments on account fix every unpaid bill?

No. A reduction needs a supported lower-liability estimate. It does not erase balancing tax already due or replace a payment arrangement.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Download the current balance and due dates.
  • Separate tax, advance payments, interest and penalties.
  • Prepare an honest affordability summary.
  • Use the official HMRC route and record agreed terms.
  • Keep filing and future tax budgeting on track.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: How to Reduce Self Assessment Payments on Account
excerpt: If this year’s Self Assessment tax will be lower than last year’s bill, you can ask HMRC to reduce payments on account. Here is when that makes sense, how to claim, and the interest risk if you cut them too far.
metaTitle: Reduce Payments on Account: Evidence and Interest Risk | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Learn when to reduce Self Assessment payments on account, what to include in your estimate and why an excessive reduction can create interest.
featuredImageAlt: A trader compares last-year accounts with a lower-income current-year forecast, cautious thoughtful adviser.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Understand your Self Assessment tax bill: Payments on account
GOV.UK — Claim to reduce payments on account
GOV.UK — Understand your Self Assessment tax bill: Overview

content:
This page is about asking HMRC to lower the advance instalments, not about what payments on account are in general. If you need the basics first, start with payments on account explained, then come back here.

When a reduction claim makes sense

GOV.UK’s claim guidance says you can apply to reduce the amounts you have been asked to pay if:

  • your business profits or other income goes down
  • the tax relief you are entitled to goes up
  • tax deducted at source is more than in the previous tax year

In plain terms: you need a realistic reason to expect this year’s Self Assessment liability to be lower than the figure HMRC used when it set the two instalments (usually half of last year’s tax, due by midnight on 31 January and 31 July).

How to claim

You can reduce payments on account:

  • Online in your HMRC account (GOV.UK’s payments-on-account page lists the “Reduce payments on account” path after you open your latest Self Assessment return), or
  • By post using form SA303, printed and sent to HMRC

You will need to give HMRC the amount you expect to make so it can recalculate the instalments. For a postal claim, GOV.UK also asks for the name and address of your HMRC office (from the top of your statement) and either your Self Assessment Unique Taxpayer Reference or an employer reference.

GOV.UK’s claim page says you must claim by 31 January after the end of the tax year. Its worked example is: claim by 31 January 2025 for the year 2023 to 2024. Check the live guidance for the year you are adjusting before you leave it late.

Interest risk if you cut them too far

If you reduce payments on account and the final bill is higher than expected, GOV.UK says you can be charged interest on the difference. That is why casual “I’ll just set them to zero” reductions are a bad idea. Use a careful estimate of the tax you expect to owe, not a hopeful guess.

Illustrative only: last year’s Self Assessment tax was £8,000, so instalments were set at £4,000 and £4,000. Mid-year your trade clearly looks closer to a £5,000 bill. Asking HMRC to reduce each instalment toward £2,500 can ease cashflow. If the year later settles at £7,000 instead, interest can apply on the underpaid advance amount. The numbers are examples, not advice for your return.

Do not confuse this with a payment plan

Reducing payments on account changes how much HMRC asks for in advance. It is not the same as a Time to Pay arrangement or Budget Payment Plan if you cannot pay a bill that is already due. Those options sit in I cannot pay my Self Assessment tax bill.

Getting the estimate right

A reduction claim is only as good as the forecast behind it. Pull year-to-date sales, rental statements, CIS deductions, payroll figures and known reliefs before you submit a number to HMRC. If an accountant prepares your return, ask them to sense-check the estimate rather than filing a reduction blind.

TaxSimba’s Self Assessment service can help prepare the return that feeds these figures. We do not guarantee HMRC will accept a particular reduction amount, and we do not promise you will avoid interest if the estimate is wrong. Re-check the current GOV.UK claim page before you submit.

Put it into practice

Update the forecast when the work returns

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A freelancer's advance instalments are £3,000 each, based on the previous year's relevant tax. A documented fall in work supports an estimated £4,000 liability, suggesting £2,000 instalments if the reduction calculation applies. Later, a large contract changes the forecast. She revisits the claim instead of leaving the lower figure untouched. The exercise concerns estimated tax, not simply a percentage fall in sales; other income, deductible costs and tax already deducted all matter.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Is the expected tax liability genuinely lower?Forecast the full relevant tax position rather than reducing instalments solely because cash is short.
What evidence supports the forecast?Keep year-to-date figures, committed work, costs and tax-deducted records.
Has the outlook changed after the claim?Review the estimate and correct an excessive reduction before the final calculation surprises you.

Two more questions you may have

Can I reduce instalments to zero?

Only if a supported liability estimate justifies it. Reducing too far can lead to interest on the difference.

Will a lower turnover always mean lower payments?

No. Profit margins, other taxable income, reliefs and tax deducted elsewhere can change the result. Estimate the liability as a whole.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Record the current instalments and tax year.
  • Prepare year-to-date income and cost totals.
  • Forecast remaining income, reliefs and tax deductions.
  • Keep the calculation supporting the requested reduction.
  • Set a review date after new work or income changes.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: Landlord Mortgage Interest Tax Relief: How Finance Costs Work Now
excerpt: Residential landlords no longer deduct mortgage interest straight from rental profit in the old way. Here is how the basic-rate finance-cost tax reduction works, what counts as a finance cost, and what records to keep.
metaTitle: Landlord Mortgage Interest: How Tax Relief Works | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Understand residential landlord mortgage interest relief, separate interest from capital repayments and prepare records for the basic-rate tax reduction.
featuredImageAlt: A landlord separates mortgage interest paperwork from a property-profit ledger, house keys visible.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Tax relief for residential landlords: how it's worked out
GOV.UK — Work out your rental income when you let property
GOV.UK — Renting out your property: Paying tax and National Insurance

content:
If you still think residential mortgage interest comes off rental profit pound for pound, the rules have moved on. For individual landlords of residential property, finance-cost relief is restricted to a basic-rate Income Tax reduction. GOV.UK’s transition finished from 6 April 2020, so the older style of full deduction from profit no longer applies for those residential finance costs.

What this page covers (and what it does not)

This is the finance-cost / mortgage-interest treatment for residential lets. It is not a full landlord Self Assessment checklist (see Self Assessment for landlords 2025/26) and not the Making Tax Digital landlord guide (MTD for landlords 2026/27).

How the tax reduction works

GOV.UK explains that the reduction is the basic rate value (currently 20%) of the lower of:

  • finance costs not deducted from rental income in the tax year (plus any finance costs brought forward)
  • property business profits for the year (after using brought-forward losses)
  • adjusted total income that exceeds your personal allowance (after losses and reliefs, excluding savings and dividends income)

The tax reduction cannot be used to create a tax refund. If the limiting figure is property profits or adjusted total income rather than finance costs, unused finance costs can be carried forward for later years’ basic-rate reductions.

What counts as a finance cost

On GOV.UK’s rental-income guidance, restricted finance costs include interest on mortgages, loans (including loans to buy furnishings), and overdrafts, plus related incidental costs of getting or repaying finance. If a loan covers both residential and commercial property, or mixes trade and residential use, you need a reasonable split. Only the residential share is restricted in this way.

GOV.UK also notes that UK and non-UK resident companies are outside this individual restriction and continue to get relief for interest in the usual way for companies. This article is aimed at individual landlords.

Why higher-rate landlords feel it more

Because residential finance costs no longer reduce taxable property profit in full, your total income for rate-band purposes can look higher even when cash interest has not changed. Relief then comes as a 20% tax reducer, not as a deduction at your higher or additional rate.

Illustrative only (adapted from GOV.UK’s published case-study style; GOV.UK’s own examples use older personal allowance and band figures for teaching, so treat them as mechanics, not current thresholds): a landlord with other income plus rental receipts can be pushed into a higher band once finance costs stop wiping profit down. The 20% reducer then covers only part of the cash interest. Your accountant needs the full interest figure either way.

Records worth keeping

  • Mortgage or loan interest statements for the tax year (interest element, not the full repayment)
  • Arrangement or exit fees tied to the finance
  • Notes if borrowing was increased or split across properties
  • Any unused finance costs brought forward from earlier years

If you want help preparing the property pages that include this relief, start from TaxSimba’s rental income tax service page and register for accountant-led Self Assessment support. We do not invent allowable finance costs or guarantee a particular tax bill. Confirm current GOV.UK wording for your lets before you file.

Put it into practice

The lender's breakdown matters

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

Jo's mortgage payments total £10,800 for the year, including £6,900 interest and £3,900 capital repayment. She supplies the interest certificate rather than claiming £10,800 as an expense. For an individual residential landlord, restricted finance costs are considered under the tax-reduction rules, with limits and possible carry-forward. The £6,900 is therefore an input to a relief calculation, not an automatic deduction from rent or a guaranteed cash refund.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Interest or repayment of borrowed capital?Obtain the lender's breakdown and exclude capital repayments from the interest figure.
Individual residential let or another structure?Confirm the owner and use of borrowing before applying the residential restriction.
Any unused finance costs from earlier years?Bring the carry-forward schedule so relief is considered consistently.

Two more questions you may have

Is relief always 20% of everything paid to the lender?

No. Capital repayments do not qualify as interest and the finance-cost reduction is subject to statutory limits. Supply the detailed figures.

Does the borrowing have to be on the rented property's mortgage?

The purpose and use of borrowing matter. Provide the loan history and how funds were used rather than deciding from the security alone.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Collect annual interest and fee statements.
  • Separate interest from capital repayments.
  • Describe the purpose and use of each loan.
  • Record mixed residential, commercial or private use.
  • Locate prior unused finance-cost schedules.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: CIS Deductions on Your Self Assessment Return: How Subcontractors Reclaim Tax
excerpt: CIS deductions are advance payments towards your tax, not a final bill. Sole trader and partner subcontractors reclaim them through Self Assessment using contractor payment and deduction statements.
metaTitle: CIS Deductions on Self Assessment: Gross Pay and Credit | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Prepare CIS figures for Self Assessment: reconcile gross contractor payments, deductions and bank receipts, then check the credit against the final tax bill.
featuredImageAlt: A construction subcontractor compares deduction statements with invoices and gross earnings, hard hat beside desk.

sources.label: GOV.UK — What you must do as a Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) subcontractor: Pay tax and claim back deductions
GOV.UK — What you must do as a Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) subcontractor: Overview
GOV.UK — Claim repayment of subcontractor deductions

content:
If contractors take CIS deductions from your pay, those amounts are advance payments towards your Income Tax and National Insurance, not a separate final tax. For sole traders and partners, the usual reclaim or set-off happens when you file your Self Assessment return.

What to put on the return

GOV.UK’s CIS subcontractor guidance says that at the end of the tax year you send your Self Assessment return as usual and record:

  • your total pay before deductions were taken, as income
  • the total deductions contractors have taken, as CIS deductions

HMRC then works out how much tax you owe and takes off the CIS deductions. If anything is still due, you pay by 31 January following the end of the tax year. If the deductions exceed what you owe, HMRC can refund the excess.

Keep the monthly payment and deduction statements your contractors give you. Without those totals, the CIS credit on the return is guesswork.

This is not the general sole-trader checklist

Wider sole-trader prep for 2025/26 sits in Self Assessment for sole traders. This page stays on CIS credit and reclaim mechanics.

In-year repayments vs waiting for the return

If you need a repayment of CIS deductions during the current tax year (rather than waiting for the year-end return), HMRC publishes form CIS40 for individuals. GOV.UK’s CIS40 page says to use your tax return instead once you are claiming after the end of the tax year. If you stop trading mid-year, GOV.UK also points sole traders and partners to an in-year claim route for deductions already taken.

Limited companies are different

Company subcontractors do not reclaim CIS through a personal Self Assessment return in the same way. GOV.UK directs companies to set CIS deductions against PAYE liabilities through FPS and EPS payroll submissions. Do not try to clear company CIS through a Corporation Tax return. This article is aimed at sole traders and partners using Self Assessment.

Gross payment status

If you have gross payment status, contractors should not take the usual CIS deductions in advance. The reclaim story on this page mainly matters when deductions have actually been taken (commonly 20% if you are registered, or 30% if you are not).

Illustrative only: a sole trader receives £40,000 gross from contractors in a year and sees £8,000 of CIS deductions on the statements. The Self Assessment trade pages still start from the £40,000 income figure, with the £8,000 entered as CIS deductions so it credits the bill. Whether that creates a balancing payment or a refund depends on the rest of the year’s tax, not on CIS alone.

CIS registration and reclaim do not, on their own, decide whether Making Tax Digital for Income Tax applies. MTD looks at qualifying self-employment and property income against HMRC’s phased thresholds. If you are unsure whether digital records and quarterly updates also apply to you, check if MTD applies before you assume CIS cash-flow is the only change.

If you want an accountant to prepare the Self Assessment pages that include CIS, use TaxSimba’s self-employed tax return service and register. Bring every payment and deduction statement you have. We do not guarantee a refund amount, and we do not replace HMRC’s CIS registration process.

Put it into practice

Keep the income and credit on separate lines

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A contractor statement shows £2,500 pay before CIS and £500 deducted, with £2,000 reaching Adeel's bank. He records the gross income and the deduction separately. He then checks every monthly statement against the year's bank entries and keeps genuine business costs in their own schedule. A £500 deduction is a tax credit to reconcile, not an expense and not a promise of a £500 refund. His final return includes the rest of his income and reliefs.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Does gross pay reconcile to net receipts plus deductions?Use contractor statements and investigate missing or inconsistent months.
Are CIS deductions recorded as a credit?Do not deduct the same amount from turnover or claim it again as a business expense.
Are you a sole trader, partner or company?Use the appropriate reclaim process; company CIS does not follow the same personal-return route.

Two more questions you may have

Will all CIS deductions be refunded?

Only any excess after the full tax calculation and relevant account checks. A balancing payment may still be due.

Can I infer deductions from the bank receipt?

A bank credit alone does not establish the gross amount or CIS deducted. Obtain the payment and deduction statement.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • List all contractors and payment months.
  • Total gross pay before CIS deductions.
  • Total evidenced deductions separately.
  • Reconcile statements to bank receipts.
  • Collect expenses and other personal tax information.

title: I Haven’t Declared Rental Income to HMRC — What Should I Do?
excerpt: If rental income was never told to HMRC, ignoring it is not a fix. Here is what GOV.UK’s Let Property Campaign covers, how notification and disclosure work at a high level, and how ongoing Self Assessment fits afterwards.
metaTitle: Undeclared Rental Income: Prepare an HMRC Disclosure | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Missed rental income? Organise records by tax year, check the Let Property Campaign route and prepare evidence for tax, interest and any penalties.
featuredImageAlt: A landlord opens older unreported rent records with an adviser and sorts a truthful year-by-year timeline.
ctaLabel: Get accountant help with your rental tax

relatedPages.label: Get accountant help with your rental tax

sources.label: GOV.UK — Let Property Campaign: your guide to making a disclosure
GOV.UK — Make a voluntary disclosure to HMRC
GOV.UK — Work out your rental income when you let property
GOV.UK — Check how to register for Self Assessment

content:
Realising rental income never reached HMRC is unsettling. Waiting and hoping is not a solution. GOV.UK asks landlords with unpaid tax on letting income to tell HMRC and put the figures right. This guide summarises the official Let Property Campaign path at a high level. It is general information, not personal tax or legal advice, and it does not assume why the income was missed.

What to do first

  1. Stop guessing. Read HMRC’s current Let Property Campaign guide on GOV.UK and check whether that route applies to you.
  2. Gather what records you still have: rent received, agent statements, bank entries, repair invoices, and finance-cost paperwork.
  3. Separate older undeclared years from current or very recent years that may still belong on a normal Self Assessment return or amendment rather than inside a disclosure pack.
  4. If the calculations span several years or the paperwork is incomplete, consider professional help before you send figures to HMRC.

What the Let Property Campaign is

HMRC describes the Let Property Campaign as a way for landlords who owe tax from letting residential property in the UK or abroad to get their tax affairs up to date. GOV.UK says individual landlords can use it for situations such as a single let, a portfolio, a room in a main home above the Rent a Room threshold, holiday lettings, inherited property that is let, and some non-resident landlords of UK property.

It does not cover landlords disclosing only non-residential property such as a shop or garage, or disclosures on behalf of a company or trust. Those situations need a different route.

Notification, disclosure and payment (high level)

GOV.UK’s process has clear stages:

  • Notify HMRC that you intend to make a disclosure as soon as you become aware you owe tax on letting income. At this stage you do not need to supply the full income figures.
  • HMRC then gives you a disclosure reference number and a payment reference number.
  • Disclose the undeclared letting income within 90 days of the date on your notification acknowledgement, and pay what you owe (or agree payment arrangements with HMRC by that same deadline if you cannot pay in full).

GOV.UK warns that if disclosure and payment (or agreed arrangements) are not completed by that deadline, you will not be able to make a disclosure under the campaign’s terms. Always use the dates on your own acknowledgement letter.

Current or prior-year income may sit on a tax return instead

HMRC’s campaign guide draws an important line: income in the current tax year should not go in the disclosure. If you are not already in Self Assessment, register now and report that income on the return HMRC issues after the year ends. Income for the year before the current tax year is also generally handled through a tax return or, if you already filed, through an amendment within the usual amendment window. Put simply, not every missed rent figure belongs in the multi-year disclosure form.

Records and incomplete paperwork

Start with bank statements, tenancy agreements, agent reports and invoices. If records are incomplete, GOV.UK says you should make your best estimate, keep your workings, and be ready to explain them. Ask your bank for copy statements early if they are missing. This is also the moment to start keeping proper property records going forward.

Tax, interest and penalties (carefully)

Any extra tax included in a disclosure is late, so GOV.UK says interest runs from the date the tax was due until it is paid. Penalties can also apply where returns were wrong or HMRC was not told about a tax liability. HMRC asks you to consider whether errors happened despite taking reasonable care, through carelessness, or deliberately. Those categories affect how many years may need to be covered and how penalties are approached. This article will not label your situation or promise any penalty outcome.

GOV.UK notes that voluntary disclosure is usually treated more favourably than waiting until HMRC finds the income another way, and that waiting can lead to higher penalties and more serious enforcement outcomes. That is HMRC’s published warning, not a prediction about you.

Why multiple years get complicated

Each year can have different rent, expenses, finance-cost rules, rate bands and other income. Losses in one year may only set against later rental profits. Joint ownership means each person usually needs their own figures and, where relevant, their own disclosure. Mixing years that belong on ordinary returns with years that belong in a disclosure makes the pack easy to get wrong.

After you bring older years up to date

Once past liabilities are addressed, future rental profit still needs correct reporting. That usually means staying in Self Assessment while it applies, keeping records, and watching Making Tax Digital for Income Tax if your property income brings you into scope. Practical prep for a normal year is in Self Assessment for landlords 2025/26; MTD timing is in MTD for landlords 2026/27.

TaxSimba provides accountant-led help with ongoing rental Self Assessment and related landlord tax compliance through our rental income tax service. We do not claim to run a specialist Let Property Campaign disclosure product on this page. If you need help getting future returns right after you have dealt with HMRC’s disclosure process, get accountant help with your rental tax. Recheck the live GOV.UK campaign guide before you act, because process details can change.

Put it into practice

Keep recent and older years apart

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A landlord discovers rent missing from several years. She builds a schedule for each year with gross rent, ownership share, expenses, finance costs and other income. She checks whether recent figures belong on an ordinary return or amendment and whether older residential letting income fits the Let Property Campaign. After notifying, she records the deadline on HMRC's acknowledgement. She does not apply today's allowances or finance-cost treatment to every historical year.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Which years and properties are affected?Create separate annual schedules with ownership and residence details.
Ordinary return, amendment or disclosure?Check the appropriate route for each year before combining figures in a campaign submission.
What deadline did HMRC give?Work from the actual acknowledgement and arrange disclosure and payment or agreed terms in time.

Two more questions you may have

Should I estimate missing records without explaining them?

No. Seek replacement evidence first, retain a reasonable reconstruction and clearly explain estimates and their basis where the official process allows them.

Does voluntary disclosure guarantee no penalty?

No. The outcome depends on the facts and applicable rules. Accurate records and timely engagement support the process without guaranteeing a result.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • List affected years, properties and ownership shares.
  • Obtain bank and letting-agent records.
  • Reconstruct income and costs year by year.
  • Check the correct reporting route for each year.
  • Record acknowledgement dates, deadlines and payment discussions.

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: Do I Need Self Assessment for a Side Hustle?
excerpt: A side hustle can trigger Self Assessment even if you already pay tax through PAYE. Here is how HMRC looks at the £1,000 trading threshold, what counts as income, and when to register.
metaTitle: Side Hustle Tax: When Self Assessment Is Needed | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check side-hustle tax using gross trading income, distinguish personal sales from a trade and prepare records alongside your PAYE employment income.
featuredImageAlt: A worker at home separates salaried-job papers from a small handmade-products side business.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Who must send a tax return
GOV.UK — Become a sole trader: Register as a sole trader
GOV.UK — Tax-free allowances on property and trading income

content:
Often, yes — if your side hustle is self-employed trading and your gross income from it is more than £1,000 in a tax year (6 April to 5 April). GOV.UK lists that as a reason you must send a Self Assessment tax return. Having a PAYE job does not cancel the need to report the side income.

What HMRC means by “more than £1,000”

The figure is usually your turnover before expenses, not profit. If you invoice £1,400 for weekend design work and spend £500 on software, you are still over £1,000 for registration purposes. Expenses may reduce taxable profit later; they do not push you back under the “who must send a return” test once gross income is over the limit.

Example only: you earn £38,000 from employment (taxed through PAYE) and £1,250 from selling handmade goods online before costs. That £1,250 is enough for GOV.UK’s self-employed filing trigger, even if profit after materials is under £1,000.

When a small side hustle may not need a return

If your annual gross trading income from one or more trades is £1,000 or less, GOV.UK’s trading-allowance guidance says you may not have to tell HMRC — unless another rule applies. You may still need to register if, for example, you want to pay voluntary Class 2 National Insurance, claim Tax-Free Childcare based on self-employment, or claim Maternity Allowance on that basis. Use HMRC’s “check if you need to send a tax return” tool when you are unsure.

Other side income that is not “trading”

Not every extra pound is a trade. Rent from a spare room or buy-to-let, tips, untaxed dividends, foreign income or capital gains can each create their own Self Assessment reasons. A side hustle that is clearly self-employment sits under the sole-trader rules; property income is different. If you are mainly letting, read Self Assessment for landlords instead of treating it as trading.

Common mistake

Waiting until January to decide. If you need a return and have not sent one before (or skipped the previous year), GOV.UK expects you to tell HMRC by 5 October after the tax year ends. That is separate from the 31 January filing and payment date. See register by 5 October.

Practical next steps

  1. Add up gross side income for the tax year, not just what landed in your personal account after costs.
  2. Keep invoices, platform statements and expense receipts from day one — even while the hustle is small.
  3. If you are over £1,000, register as a sole trader through Self Assessment and diary the filing deadline.
  4. If you are near the line, read the £1,000 trading allowance before assuming nothing needs reporting.

TaxSimba’s Self Assessment service is accountant-led: we help gather the side income and employment picture and file correctly. We do not promise a particular tax bill or that every small activity is exempt. If you are ready for help, start Self Assessment with TaxSimba.

Put it into practice

Low profit does not change the gross-income test

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

Tessa earns £1,600 from weekend illustration commissions and spends £900 on relevant costs. She compares the £1,600 gross trading receipts with the filing trigger rather than using £700 after costs. Her PAYE job does not automatically settle this separate income. She keeps invoices, expense evidence and her employment documents, then checks whether the trading allowance or actual allowable costs are appropriate on the return. The example does not calculate the final tax.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Is the activity trading or something else?Describe what you sell or do and how the activity operates before applying a trading allowance.
What is total gross trading income?Add relevant trades for the tax year before expenses or platform deductions.
Do other reporting reasons apply?Check property, gains and other untaxed income as well as the side activity.

Two more questions you may have

Does PAYE mean I cannot need Self Assessment?

No. PAYE covers employment deductions; separate trading income or another tax reason can still require a return.

Do sales of my own used possessions always count as a trade?

No. Disposing of personal items differs from trading. Keep context and check capital-gains rules for valuable items where relevant.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Describe the activity and when it began.
  • Total gross receipts across relevant trades.
  • Reconcile platform fees and net payouts.
  • Keep actual expense evidence for comparison.
  • Gather PAYE documents and check registration requirements.

No. PAYE covers employment deductions; separate trading income or another tax reason can still require a return.
Do sales of my own used possessions always count as a trade?
No. Disposing of personal items differs from trading. Keep context and check capital-gains rules for valuable items where relevant.

title: Trading Allowance £1,000: Do I Still Need to Tell HMRC?
excerpt: The £1,000 trading allowance can make small amounts of trading income tax-free, but it is not a blanket “ignore HMRC” rule. Here is when you can stay silent, when you must register, and when claiming the allowance on a return is better than expenses.
metaTitle: £1,000 Trading Allowance: Income, Expenses and Limits | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check how the £1,000 trading allowance works, compare it with actual expenses and avoid treating it as a separate allowance for every side hustle.
featuredImageAlt: A maker considers small gross sales against expense receipts, calculator and modest product boxes, no exact amounts.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Tax-free allowances on property and trading income
GOV.UK — Become a sole trader: Register as a sole trader
GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Who must send a tax return

content:
Sometimes you do not. GOV.UK says that if your annual gross trading income from one or more trades is £1,000 or less, you may not have to tell HMRC. That £1,000 figure is also the maximum trading allowance you can use as tax-free relief when the rules allow it. The catch: several situations still force a Self Assessment return, and once your gross income is over £1,000 you must register.

Two different uses of the £1,000 figure

  • Registration / “do I need a return?” — Sole traders who earn more than £1,000 before reliefs generally must register for Self Assessment.
  • Trading allowance on a return — If you already file, you can often deduct up to £1,000 from gross trading income instead of claiming actual expenses. You cannot claim both the full allowance and those expenses on the same income.

There is a separate £1,000 property allowance for property income. Trading and property each have their own £1,000 pot if you have both.

When you must still tell HMRC under £1,000

GOV.UK’s allowance guidance says you must register and declare the income if, for example, you:

  • want to claim loss relief on a return
  • want to pay voluntary Class 2 National Insurance
  • want Tax-Free Childcare based on self-employment income
  • want Maternity Allowance based on self-employment

Those are policy choices about benefits and National Insurance, not optional “nice to have” paperwork. If any apply, do not rely on the silent under-£1,000 path.

If you earn more than £1,000

You must register for Self Assessment (GOV.UK ties this to the 5 October date after the tax year for people who need to tell HMRC). On the return you can usually either:

  • deduct the £1,000 trading allowance from gross income, or
  • claim actual allowable expenses (and capital allowances where relevant) instead

Illustrative only: gross freelance income £3,200; receipts £400. Claiming the £1,000 allowance leaves £2,200 taxable trading income. Claiming £400 expenses leaves £2,800. The allowance wins here — but if expenses were £1,500, claiming expenses would usually be better. Work both ways before you tick a box.

What this means if you already file Self Assessment

Being in Self Assessment for another reason (employment benefits, property, high income) does not stop you using the trading allowance on trading income, where the rules allow it. It does mean you report the activity on the return rather than staying invisible under the small-income exemption.

Common mistake

Mixing up profit with gross income. The registration test and the allowance both start from gross trading receipts. A loss-making hustle with £2,000 of sales is still over £1,000 for “must register” purposes.

For side-hustle context see Do I need Self Assessment for a side hustle?. TaxSimba’s Self Assessment accountants can help choose between the allowance and expenses on a live return. We do not guarantee which option saves more tax in your case. Start Self Assessment with TaxSimba when you want that review done properly.

Put it into practice

Compare the two methods before choosing

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

Milo has £2,800 gross receipts from eligible trading and £1,200 of allowable costs. Deducting actual costs would leave £1,600; using a £1,000 allowance would leave £1,800. He checks eligibility and the wider facts before choosing. He cannot claim both deductions against the same income, and several trades do not give him a fresh £1,000 allowance for each one. This arithmetic compares trading-income figures, not his final tax bill.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Is this income eligible for the allowance?Check exclusions and special relationships before choosing the simplified deduction.
Do actual allowable costs exceed the allowance?Compare both permitted methods using supported figures and relevant capital costs.
Are there several trades?Apply the allowance rules across the relevant income rather than duplicating the allowance per activity.

Two more questions you may have

Can the allowance create a trading loss?

No. If you need to claim a loss, check the actual-expense route and applicable loss-relief rules.

Is the threshold measured after expenses?

No. Start from gross trading income. A small profit does not make gross receipts above £1,000 disappear for registration purposes.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Total eligible gross trading receipts.
  • Check excluded sources or connected-party circumstances.
  • Calculate actual allowable costs separately.
  • Compare allowance and actual-cost outcomes.
  • Record registration, benefit or loss-relief reasons requiring a return.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: How to Amend a Self Assessment Tax Return
excerpt: Spotted a mistake after filing? You can usually correct a Self Assessment return within 12 months of the deadline. Here is the online process, the 72-hour wait, and what to do if the amendment window has closed.
metaTitle: Amend a Self Assessment Return: Dates and Evidence | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Need to correct Self Assessment? Identify the tax year, check the amendment window and keep evidence of the changed figures and revised calculation.
featuredImageAlt: A taxpayer and accountant correct one marked entry on a copy of a previously completed return, keep original beside it.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: If you need to change your return
GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Deadlines

content:
GOV.UK lets you change a Self Assessment tax return after you have filed it — for example if you missed income, overstated expenses or used the wrong box. For most people the clean route is an online amendment within 12 months of the Self Assessment deadline for that year.

How long you have

You can correct a return within 12 months of the Self Assessment deadline, online or by sending another paper return. That window is tied to the normal filing deadline for the year, not to the day you happened to submit early. Example: for a return whose online deadline was 31 January 2026, the usual amendment cut-off is 31 January 2027. Always check GOV.UK for the year you are correcting.

Online amendments (HMRC account)

GOV.UK says you must wait 3 days (72 hours) after filing before you can update the return online. Then:

  1. Sign in to your HMRC account
  2. Open your Self Assessment account
  3. Choose More Self Assessment details → At a glance → Tax return options
  4. Select the tax year, open the return, correct it and file again

If you filed through commercial software, contact the software provider first; GOV.UK says to contact HMRC if the software cannot make corrections.

Paper amendments

If you need to amend on paper, GOV.UK tells you to mark “amendment” on each page and include your name and Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR), then send the corrected pages to the address on your Self Assessment paperwork.

If the 12-month window has passed

You cannot use the normal online or paper amendment route. GOV.UK says you must write to HMRC explaining what is wrong. That is a slower, more formal path — get your figures and evidence straight before you write. An amendment is not the same as a voluntary disclosure for income you never reported at all; older undeclared rental income, for example, may belong on a different HMRC process (see undeclared rental income).

After you amend

Your tax calculation can change. You may owe more (with a new payment date and possible interest) or be due a refund. Pay any extra on time; if you cannot, read I cannot pay my Self Assessment tax bill rather than ignoring the revised balance.

Common mistake

Amending only the final tax figure “to make it look right” without fixing the income and expense boxes that drive the calculation. Correct the source figures and let HMRC’s calculation rebuild.

TaxSimba’s Self Assessment service can help rebuild a correct return and decide whether an amendment or another HMRC route fits. We cannot promise HMRC will accept every correction without follow-up questions. Start Self Assessment with TaxSimba if you want an accountant to handle the change with you.

Put it into practice

Correct the box that caused the mistake

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

Ruth discovers an omitted £650 business receipt after filing early. She checks the amendment deadline for that tax year, preserves the original submission and records why turnover changes. She uses the appropriate amendment route and retains the new filing confirmation and calculation. She then checks the account for additional tax and interest. Editing her spreadsheet alone would not amend the submitted return, and changing only the final tax figure would not repair the source error.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Is the normal amendment window still open?Check the tax year's statutory deadline rather than counting a year from early submission.
Which source figures need correction?Keep the original, corrected values and evidence for the change.
Was the correction actually submitted?Retain confirmation and check the revised calculation and payment position.

Two more questions you may have

Can I amend in HMRC's portal after filing through software?

Check the software provider's correction route first. Follow HMRC guidance if that route cannot make the required amendment.

What if the ordinary window has closed?

Use the appropriate written HMRC process for the correction or claim. Time limits and required statements differ, so identify the exact issue before sending it.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Record tax year and original submission reference.
  • Check the applicable amendment or claim deadline.
  • List original and corrected values with evidence.
  • Submit through the appropriate route and retain confirmation.
  • Check the revised tax, interest and payment dates.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.
